background_notes.fact: If (m_i) indexed by the finite set I is an integer basis of M and also a complex basis of V, then R⊗_ℤ M has R-basis (1⊗m_i). The map r⊗m↦rm into V is injective, has image the R-span of M, and its image spans V over ℂ. Here |I|=n, so its R-rank is n.

background_notes.justification: Finite basis exchange gives equality of the cardinalities of the two complex bases. Write a_i:M→ℤ for the integer coordinate maps for m. The maps r⊗m↦r a_i(m) are well-defined by bilinearity and give an inverse to (r_i)↦∑r_i⊗m_i. The map into V sends this sum to ∑r_i m_i, which vanishes only if every coefficient vanishes, by complex independence and R⊂ℂ. Its image is precisely the finite R-linear combinations of M, contains each m_i, and hence has complex span V. This elaborates the coordinate construction already displayed in S001.

background_notes.fact: For a prime p and integers 0≤j≤λ<p, the integer c=binom(λ,j) is not divisible by p and is a unit in R=ℤ_(p), with inverse 1/c∈R.

grounds.reason: A rational with denominator not divisible by p belongs to R.
S002 uses the integer identity c j!(λ−j)!=λ!.

background_notes.justification: Each positive factor in these factorials is less than p and therefore coprime to p; the Euclidean algorithm gives an inverse for its residue modulo p. Products of these invertible residues remain invertible, including the empty product 1. Thus p does not divide λ!. If p divided c, the displayed integer identity would force p to divide λ!, a contradiction. Consequently c≠0 and the fraction 1/c satisfies the defining denominator condition for R; its product with c is 1.
